tests.notes: unsigned >> is a logical shift; zeros are shifted in from the left
signed >> is an arithmetic shift that replicates the sign bit; a converter must lower it to ashr, not lshr
-7 >> 1 == -4 (rounds toward negative infinity) while -7 / 2 == -3 (truncates toward zero)
compiles successfully; << discards overflowed bits silently while a * 2 reverts with Panic(0x11) for type(uint256).max
unsigned shifts by an amount >= the bit width yield 0 and never revert; native LLVM shifts are undefined for such amounts, so a converter must handle it explicitly
arithmetic right shift of a signed value by >= its width yields -1 for negative values and 0 otherwise
the shift amount may be any unsigned type; the result type follows the left operand only
<< on a signed value shifts the two's complement pattern with no overflow check; int8 64 << 1 == -128
since 0.7.0 a literal shifted by a non-literal is computed in uint256 (non-negative) or int256 (negative)
uint8(1) << n computes in uint8 so high bits are discarded at 8 bits; the uncast form is rejected in 018
bytesN supports << and >> with an unsigned bit-count; the result keeps the bytesN type
literal << literal is folded at compile time to an exact constant, which converts as long as the value fits the target type
shift amounts must be unsigned; a negative literal amount is rejected
a signed shift amount is rejected even with an unsigned left operand
1 << 256 is folded to 2**256 which does not fit uint256; the non-literal form silently yields 0 at runtime (see 006)
1 << n is computed in uint256, so assigning it to uint8 is an implicit narrowing; fix is uint8(1) << n (see 012)
shift operators do not apply to bool
shift operators do not apply to address directly; an explicit conversion to uint160 is needed
